newsitem.title: INDIA: Reining Indian money supply growth seen tough job.
newsitem.headline: Reining Indian money supply growth seen tough job.

text.p: India's central bank has a tough job trying to keep money supply within targets with foreign capital inflows continuing unabated and the government delaying a long-pending hike in petroleum prices, analysts said on Wednesday.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor C. Rangarajan on Monday reiterated the central bank's commitment to maintaining the money supply growth in the 15.0-15.5 percent target.
The M3 money supply growth rose to 16.6 percent on June 6 compared with 16.4 percent on May 23, according to latest figures released by the RBI.
"The key to both (controlling) money supply as well as rupee's depreciation is in the oil price hike," Chetan Ahya, analyst at Caspian Research said.
He said state-run oil firms have been raising offshore loans to pay for oil imports as the government has not reimbursed billions of rupees it owed these firms for the oil subsidy.

The oil price hike will raise revenues for oil firms who could then buy dollars from the local inter-bank market to fund imports, Ahya said. The resultant spurt in dollar demand will also help depreciate the overvalued Indian rupee, he added.

The RBI has been conducting regular repo auctions in recent months to mop up excess liquidity with banks but this is not sustainable over a long period, Anindya Chatterjee, economist at NatWest Markets, said.
Large capital inflows combined with RBI's dollar purchases from the market to arrest the rupee's appreciation have been fuelling money supply growth in recent months, analysts said.
India's foreign currency reserves rose to $24.88 billion on June 20, 1997, from $17.13 billion in June 1996.
Banks, flush with funds because of growing deposits and poor credit offtake, have been investing heavily in government securities and parking funds with RBI through repo auctions.

RBI's decision last week to cut the benchmark bank rate and the one-year deposit rate will also help to push down yields and reduce speculative inflows into the debt market, money market dealers said.
The RBI could control the money supply growth through several measures -- but each of them will be a difficult choice, French bank Societe Generale said in a India commentary.
It said the RBI could suspend its intervention in the foreign exchange market, but it would not be in the interest of Indian exporters.
The government could issue fresh bonds to mop up liquidity, but over 50 percent of the budgeted borrowing programme is already over in the first quarter of 1996/97 (April-March).
The RBI could impose cash reserve requirement on expatriate Indians' foreign currency-denominated deposits, the bank said.
This may lead to a slowdown in expatriate Indians' deposits but such a move will not be welcomed by overseas Indians or banks, analysts said.
